en: Udāna 6.6 Tatiyanānātitthiyasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, many ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects were residing in Sāvatthī, holding diverse views, diverse inclinations, diverse tastes, and dependent upon diverse doctrinal positions.
Among them, some ascetics and brahmins held such doctrines and such views:
“The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain.
Furthermore, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Both the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The self and the world are self-made; this alone is the truth, all else is vain.”
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
"The self and the world are created by another; this alone is true, all else is false.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Both self-made and other-made; both the self and the world: this alone is true, all else is vain.
Yet there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Neither self-made nor other-made; arisen by chance, both the self and the world: this alone is true, all else is vain.”
There are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Pleasure and pain, the self, and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are other recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Pleasure and pain, the self and the world, are finite; this alone is true, all else is false.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Pleasure and pain, the self and the world, are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view:
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal are pleasure and pain, the self, and the world; this alone is true, all else is false.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view: [and so forth].
“Pleasure and pain are self-made; both the self and the world are [self-made]. This alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Pleasure and pain are made by another; both the self and the world are made by another. This alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
"Both pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another; the self and the world are both self-made and made by another; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are other ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Pleasure and pain are produced neither by oneself nor by another, but have arisen fortuitously; both the self and the world are thus. This alone is the truth, all else is false.
Having fallen into quarreling, strife, and dispute, they dwell piercing one another with verbal darts, saying:
“The Dhamma is like this, it is not like that!”
“Such is the Dhamma, such is the Dhamma.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed themselves, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returning from their almsround, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

“Here, Bhante, many ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects are residing in Sāvatthī, holding various views, various inclinations, various preferences, and relying on various doctrinal positions.
Among them, some ascetics and brahmins hold such a doctrine and such a view:”

‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’ … [and so on] … having become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute, they dwell stabbing one another with the weapons of the mouth:
‘The Dhamma is thus, it is not thus; the Dhamma is otherwise than that.’
“‘Such is the Dhamma, such is the Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless.
They do not know what is beneficial and they do not know what is harmful; they do not know the Dhamma and they do not know what is contrary to the Dhamma.”

Not knowing what is beneficial and not knowing what is harmful, not knowing what is Dhamma and not knowing what is non-Dhamma, they live engaged in quarrels, engaged in strife, fallen into disputes, piercing one another with verbal weapons, saying:
“The Dhamma is like this, it is not like that;
the Dhamma is not like this, it is like that.”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“This generation is intent upon the notion of ‘I,’ and is bound up with the notion of ‘another.’”
Some did not recognize this;
they did not see it as a dart. But for one who perceives this dart as it truly is, [it is removed].
"It is I who act"—this does not occur to him;
"another acts"—this does not occur to him.
This generation is possessed by conceit.
Bound by conceit, fettered by conceit,
and engaged in contentious talk regarding views,
one does not transcend saṃsāra.
The sixth.
